analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for low earners and long-term beneficiaries, funded by higher payroll taxes on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have increased Social Security benefits in several ways: a higher minimum benefit for people who worked many years at low wages (counting years spent caring for young children), an extra benefit bump for people who have been receiving benefits for 16 or more years, and child benefits extended to full-time college students under 22. To pay for it, payroll taxes would rise gradually starting in 2017, and — the big change — earnings above the Social Security wage cap would no longer be exempt: they would be taxed for Social Security at a shrinking percentage each year until fully covered after 2026. It also ensured the new benefit increases wouldn't disqualify recipients from other assistance like Medicaid or SNAP. It never received so much as a hearing in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifelong low-wage workers, who would get a guaranteed minimum Social Security benefit tied to the poverty line; people who have collected benefits for 16 or more years, who would get a growing boost the longer they receive benefits; students whose disabled or deceased parent's benefits currently stop at 19; and the low-income beneficiaries protected from losing other aid because of the increase. The financing falls on the roughly top slice of earners, whose wages above the annual cap ($118,500 in 2015) would be taxed and whose payroll tax rate would rise from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2022.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the special minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, based on years worked (with caregiving years counted), up to 100% of the federal poverty guideline
Increases benefits by up to 5% for beneficiaries who have been receiving them for 16 or more years, so the oldest and longest-retired beneficiaries see the largest gains
Extends child's benefits for full-time post-secondary students up to age 22, helping surviving and disabled workers' children stay in college

Ensures the new benefit increases do not count as income for other federal and state assistance programs, so beneficiaries do not lose Medicaid, SNAP, or housing help because their Social Security check grew

analysis.who_pays: High earners: payroll tax rates rise gradually (to 6.5% for employees and employers, 13.0% for the self-employed by 2022) and, more significantly, wages above the Social Security tax cap become taxable in a growing share each year until fully taxed after 2026. Employers also pay the higher rate on wages up to the cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: The bill raises payroll taxes, which fall on every working person's paycheck, not only on high earners: the employee rate would rise from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2022 and employers would face the same increase, which can translate into lower wages or hiring
Extending child benefits to age 22 for post-secondary students adds a new ongoing cost to the program that the bill's financing must cover

Social Security's long-term financing shortfall is debated, and critics of expansion bills argue that raising taxes and benefits simultaneously locks in higher program costs; the bill did not get a committee hearing where such objections could be weighed

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a meaningful anti-poverty improvement: a higher minimum benefit for lifelong low earners, benefits that grow for long-term beneficiaries, student benefits, and a protection against means-tested program clawbacks, financed by a progressive tax falling overwhelmingly on high earners [S2][S3]. The main cost falls on high earners, whose payroll tax rate would rise gradually and whose earnings above the cap would increasingly be taxed [S3]. The cost to the broader public is modest: payroll taxes fund benefits, so combined employee and employer rates rising to 15.3% from 12.4% over five years is a real but gradual increase, spread across all workers and employers [S3]. The design is targeted and phased-in; the objection is less about poor design than about the tax increase itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it, so it never reached a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the bill on April 13, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
On April 21, 2015, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death, but the people shielded from any cost are the highest earners, whose wages above the Social Security cap would have faced new taxation, and employers facing a slightly higher payroll tax.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 21, 2015, and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no known Republican support — one Democratic cosponsor — but no party ever voted on it, so the record shows only that the Democratic-controlled committee did not act, not how votes would have split.

industries.industry: Highest earners (wages above the Social Security cap)
industries.note: They would pay Social Security tax on more of their income and at a higher rate, with no corresponding benefit increase tied to that extra tax. This is the group the financing burden falls on.
Their self-employment tax rate would rise to 13.0% by 2022 and apply above the contribution base, a direct cost to professionals and business owners with high reported earnings.

All employers would pay a modestly higher payroll tax rate (up 0.1 points per year to 6.5% by 2022), though only on the first wage cap; higher-earning employees would additionally be taxed above the cap on the employer side. Small relative to wages but broad.
